sentences.text: Net interest income plus noninterest income rose from $21.0 billion in FY2016 to $28.5 billion in FY2025, a 3.5% CAGR [D5][D219].
The path was not smooth: revenue was flat at roughly $22.7 billion in FY2021, then jumped 15.8% in FY2023 to $28.0 billion [D117][D169][D189].
That FY2023 step came from higher rates on earning assets and the MUB acquisition, partly offset by deposit mix and pricing [P33].
FY2024 gave back 2.4% as net interest income fell 6.4% on higher rates pressuring deposit mix and pricing [D214][D209][P21].
FY2025 recovered 4.4% to $28.5 billion, with net interest income up 2.2% and noninterest income up 7.6% [D239][D219][D234][D235].
Consumer and Business Banking was the largest segment at 31.0% of FY2025 revenue but shrank 3.9%, subtracting 1.3pp from growth [D251][D252][D253].
Its net revenue fell on deposit mix changes and second-quarter loan sales, partly offset by higher mortgage banking revenue [P6].
Payment Services grew 5.4% to 25.8% of revenue and contributed 1.4pp, with net interest income up on loan growth and lower funding costs [D260][D259][D261][P4].
Noninterest income growth of 7.6% outpaced net interest income's 2.2%, lifting fee income to $11.9 billion [D235][D234][F20].
Net income grew 20.2% against 4.4% revenue growth, and EPS grew 21.9% as the diluted share count slipped 0.2% [D227][D239][D228][D237].
The efficiency ratio was 59.0% in FY2025, below its 59.3% window median and far under the 67.4% FY2023 high [D220][D277][D276].
Noninterest expense fell 2.0% to $16.8 billion, reflecting prior-year merger and FDIC charges, lower compensation and cost savings from operational efficiencies [D238][X135][P10].
The FY2023 spike to 67.4% came from a 26.6% expense increase driven by MUB merger costs and a $734 million FDIC special assessment [D170][D188][P30].
The credit-loss provision was 7.7% of revenue, near the 6.1% peer median, and fell 2.3% on improved credit quality and loan sales [D221][D285][P12].
Net income was 26.5% of revenue against a 20.2% tax rate, so the below-the-line drag was modest [D223][D215].
Operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure for a bank, so capital return is the better test [D216].
Buybacks plus dividends of $3.7 billion were 48.3% of FY2025 net income, up from $2.8 billion in FY2022 [D218][F30][D142].
Dividends of $3.2 billion dominated that mix while buybacks were only $489 million, versus $4.5 billion in FY2019 [X95][X85][X79].
Stock-based compensation of $235 million was just 2.9% of operating cash flow, so dilution pressure stayed small [X37][D217].
Shareholders' equity rose 11.3% to $65.2 billion in FY2025, lifting return on average equity to 12.2% [D233][F114][D226].
That return ranked in the 71st percentile of seven bank peers against an 11.8% median [D282][D283].
Loans were 73.5% of deposits, up from 71.8%, as deposits grew 0.8% to $522 billion and loans 3.1% to $384 billion [D224][D199][X212][X211][X202][X201].
The allowance held at 2.0% of loans, and long-term debt is not reported after FY2022, so leverage beyond that year cannot be tracked [D225][R2][X172].
Long-term debt stops being reported after FY2022 at $39.8 billion, a data break that blocks any leverage trend past that year [R2][X172].
Revenue declined 2.4% in FY2024 as net interest income fell 6.4% on deposit mix and pricing, a one-year dip now reversed [R1][D214][D209][P21].
The efficiency ratio's 67.4% FY2023 peak was driven by one-off MUB and FDIC charges and has since fallen to 59.0%, so it looks benign [D276][D220][P30].
If the efficiency ratio stays below the 59.3% window median in the FY2026 10-K, the cost trend described here holds [D277].
A net interest income print above FY2025's $16.6 billion would confirm the 2.2% recovery; a drop below it would reverse it [F10][D234].
Watch whether long-term debt reappears in the FY2026 filing, since its absence after FY2022 leaves the leverage picture incomplete [R2][X172].
